blocks.text: If you only set one early alarm in Bondi, make it for sunrise. Because the beach faces almost due east onto the Pacific, the sun climbs straight out of the ocean — no suburbs or headland in the way, just the horizon and a slow build of colour. Sunset works differently here: the sun drops behind the land to the west, so you won't see it sink into the sea, but the afterglow on the cliffs is worth staying for. Below is where I stand for both.

blocks.text: The whole eastern edge is a front-row seat, but a few spots lift it from lovely to unforgettable — each with a different foreground.

From the clifftop lookout at the southern end — the first headland on the Bondi to Bronte coastal walk — you look back north across the whole arc of sand as the sun lifts over the water beyond Ben Buckler. During the migration months (roughly May to November) you've a real chance of spotting humpback whales offshore.

You don't need to swim to get the shot every visitor wants: the ocean pool in the foreground, waves washing its edge, sky on fire behind. Stand on the promenade above the pool at the south end. If you want to swim laps at first light, check the Bondi Icebergs website for current session times, which change seasonally.

The northern end is calmer and far less photographed. The rock shelves below the North Bondi headland and around Ben Buckler give you crashing surf against an open eastern horizon — a peaceful alternative when the south corner gets crowded.

Sunrise shifts a lot through the year — earliest around midsummer, latest in deep winter, a swing of well over an hour. Rather than trust a number I'd get wrong for your date, I check the free Geoscience Australia sunrise calculator the night before. Whatever it says, arrive 30–40 minutes earlier: the richest colour comes well before the sun clears the horizon, and clifftop parking fills fast on clear mornings.
The best mornings often have a few clouds about, not perfectly clear skies — high cloud holds the pink and gold long after a bare sky goes flat.
You don't need a fancy camera — I've shot some of my favourite Bondi frames on a phone. Timing and where you point it matter far more.

items: Shoot the blue hour first — the 20–30 minutes before the sun appears give deep blues and soft pinks, often prettier than the sunrise itself.
Use a foreground: the Icebergs pool, a rock shelf or the promenade rail gives the eye something to hold.
On a phone, tap the bright sky and drag the exposure down, so the colour stays rich and the sand falls to silhouette.
Keep the horizon level and low, and brace your phone on the promenade wall in low light.

blocks.title: Mind the edge and the swell
blocks.text: The clifftop lookouts are unfenced, and the rock platforms below can be swept by sudden waves on a big swell. Stay well back from the edge, keep off wet rock in low light, and never turn your back on the surf for a photo.

As I said, you won't see the sun sink into the sea here, so chase the afterglow instead. As it drops at your back, the eastern sky turns lilac and rose while the cliffs and the pale Icebergs building light up gold. Marks Park, on the grassy clifftop just past Mackenzies Point, is my go-to — spread a picnic, face the sea, and watch the colour deepen. To watch the sun actually drop below the horizon, Sydney's west-facing harbour spots do it far better.

items.q: Can you watch the sun set over the ocean at Bondi Beach?
items.a: No — Bondi faces east, so the sun rises over the water and sets behind the suburbs to the west. Come at sunrise for the sun-over-ocean show; at sunset, watch the pink afterglow on the eastern sky and cliffs instead.

items.q: What's the best spot for sunrise at Bondi?
items.a: My pick is Mackenzies Point, the south headland at the start of the Bondi to Bronte walk, for the view back across the whole beach. The promenade above Bondi Icebergs is best for the classic ocean-pool photo; North Bondi is quieter.

items.q: What time is sunrise at Bondi?
items.a: It shifts through the year, earliest around midsummer and latest in winter. Rather than guess, check Geoscience Australia's free sunrise calculator for your date, then arrive 30–40 minutes early.

items.q: Might I see whales while watching the sunrise?
items.a: Possibly, roughly May to November during the humpback migration. Mackenzies Point is one of the better clifftop vantage points — bring binoculars and scan the horizon while you wait.

blocks.text: Whichever end you choose, do yourself one favour: put the phone down for the last few minutes. There's a particular hush at Bondi as the sky turns — joggers slow, surfers sit up on their boards, the whole beach holding its breath. That's the bit you'll actually remember.
